Transaction.markdown: A group of statements the database treats as one unit: either all of its effects become visible (COMMIT) or none do (ROLLBACK or abort).

Schedule.markdown: The order in which statements from concurrent transactions reach the database. A schedule is *serializable* if its outcome equals some one-at-a-time order of the same transactions.

Serializable.markdown: The strongest isolation guarantee: the result is the same as if the committed transactions had run one after another in some order.

Isolation level.markdown: A promise about which concurrency anomalies a transaction can observe. Names are standardized by ANSI SQL, but products implement them differently.

Snapshot isolation.markdown: Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot taken when it starts; a write to a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction aborts (first-updater-wins). Prevents most anomalies but allows write skew.

SSI.markdown: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: snapshot isolation plus tracking of read/write dependencies. A transaction that would close a dependency cycle aborts. PostgreSQL uses it for SERIALIZABLE.

MVCC.markdown: Multi-version concurrency control: writers create new row versions instead of overwriting, so readers can see an older consistent version without waiting. Old versions are cleaned up later (VACUUM, purge).

Two-phase locking.markdown: Acquire locks while running, release none until commit (strict 2PL). Guarantees serializability (with predicate locks for phantoms) at the cost of blocking and deadlocks.

Predicate lock.markdown: A lock on the set of rows matching a condition, including rows that do not exist yet. Real engines approximate it with index-range locks (InnoDB next-key/gap locks).

Deadlock.markdown: Transactions waiting for each other's locks in a cycle. The database detects the cycle and aborts one victim, which the application must retry.

OCC.markdown: Run without locks, buffer writes, and validate at commit that nothing read has changed; abort on conflict. Cheap when conflicts are rare, wasteful on hot rows.

First-updater-wins.markdown: The snapshot-isolation rule that a transaction may not write a row that a concurrent transaction already changed and committed after its snapshot. The later writer aborts.

Lost update.markdown: Two read-modify-write cycles on the same row overlap, and the later commit overwrites the earlier one's change.

Dirty write.markdown: Overwriting a value that another transaction wrote but has not committed. Forbidden at every isolation level, including Read Uncommitted, usually by holding write locks until commit.

Dirty read.markdown: Reading data written by a transaction that has not committed (and may roll back).

Write skew.markdown: Two transactions read overlapping data, then write disjoint rows based on what they read. Each is valid alone; together they violate an invariant. Allowed by snapshot isolation.

Phantom.markdown: A row that appears in (or vanishes from) the result of a repeated query because another transaction inserted or deleted a matching row.

Read skew.markdown: Reading related rows from two different database states, so derived values (like a total) are inconsistent even though every read was of committed data.

Conflict graph.markdown: Nodes are committed transactions; an edge T1 → T2 means T1 must come before T2 in any equivalent serial order (ww, wr or rw conflict on some row). A cycle means the schedule is not serializable.

SELECT … FOR UPDATE.markdown: A read that takes an exclusive row lock, so a later write in the same transaction cannot be lost to a concurrent writer.

-- Dirty write: Alice (T1, buyer 1) and Bob (T2, buyer 2) buy the same car: each writes the buyer into the listing and the invoice.
-- Each session runs in its own connection; the lab interleaves their statements.

-- ── Session T1 ──────────────────────────────
BEGIN;  -- isolation level chosen in the lab
UPDATE cars SET v = :v WHERE id = 'listing';  -- listing = 1, computed in the app
UPDATE cars SET v = :v WHERE id = 'invoice';  -- invoice = 1, computed in the app
COMMIT;

-- ── Session T2 ──────────────────────────────
BEGIN;  -- isolation level chosen in the lab
UPDATE cars SET v = :v WHERE id = 'listing';  -- listing = 2, computed in the app
UPDATE cars SET v = :v WHERE id = 'invoice';  -- invoice = 2, computed in the app
COMMIT;

-- Write skew: Alice and Bob each check that two doctors are on call, then take themselves off call.
-- Each session runs in its own connection; the lab interleaves their statements.

-- ── Session T1 ──────────────────────────────
BEGIN;  -- isolation level chosen in the lab
SELECT SUM(v) FROM doctors WHERE tag = 'oncall';
-- app: if oncall >= 2 continue, else ROLLBACK
UPDATE doctors SET v = :v WHERE id = 'alice';  -- alice = 0, computed in the app
COMMIT;

-- ── Session T2 ──────────────────────────────
BEGIN;  -- isolation level chosen in the lab
SELECT SUM(v) FROM doctors WHERE tag = 'oncall';
-- app: if oncall >= 2 continue, else ROLLBACK
UPDATE doctors SET v = :v WHERE id = 'bob';  -- bob = 0, computed in the app
COMMIT;

"""Retry a transaction when the database aborts it (PostgreSQL, psycopg 3).

Under Repeatable Read and Serializable, PostgreSQL resolves conflicts by
aborting one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure) or
40P01 (deadlock_detected). The aborted work left no effect, so the client
must run the WHOLE transaction again, reading fresh data.
"""
import random
import time

import psycopg
from psycopg import errors

RETRYABLE = (errors.SerializationFailure, errors.DeadlockDetected)


def withdraw(conn: psycopg.Connection, account: str, amount: int) -> None:
    with conn.transaction():  # BEGIN
        balance = conn.execute("SELECT v FROM accounts WHERE id = %s", (account,)).fetchone()[0]
        conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET v = %s WHERE id = %s", (balance - amount, account))
    # leaving the block COMMITs; an exception inside it ROLLs BACK


def run_with_retry(conn: psycopg.Connection, fn, *args, attempts: int = 5):
    for attempt in range(1, attempts + 1):
        try:
            return fn(conn, *args)
        except RETRYABLE:
            # The transaction was aborted: nothing it did is visible. Back off, then rerun it from the top.
            if attempt == attempts:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, 0.01 * 2**attempt))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with psycopg.connect("dbname=lab") as conn:
        conn.isolation_level = psycopg.IsolationLevel.SERIALIZABLE
        run_with_retry(conn, withdraw, "A", 30)

scenes.title: Concurrency Anomalies
scenes.description: Interleave two transactions with no isolation and watch each classic anomaly happen.
scenes.markdown:
### What goes wrong without isolation

Each scenario is two (or three) short transactions and a **schedule**: the order in which their statements reach the database. Here the engine provides **no isolation at all** — reads see the newest value even if it is uncommitted, and writes overwrite each other — so every interleaving problem shows up.

| Anomaly | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Dirty write** | A transaction overwrites another's **uncommitted** write. Rollback no longer has a clean "before" value, and rows written together end up mixed. |
| **Lost update** | Two read-modify-writes of the same row; the later commit erases the earlier, already **committed** one. |
| **Dirty read** | A transaction uses data that another transaction wrote and later rolled back. |
| **Non-repeatable read** | Reading the same row twice in one transaction gives two values. |
| **Read skew** | Two reads of related rows come from two different database states. |
| **Phantom read** | Re-running the same query returns a new row. |
| **Write skew** | Two transactions each check a rule, then update *different* rows; together they break the rule. |

**The board.** *Sessions* (top) shows each transaction's statements: blue ran, **white** is running now, amber is waiting, green committed, red aborted, magenta caused an anomaly. *Storage* (right) shows every version of every row. *Conflict graph* records, for committed transactions, who must come before whom.

**Edit the schedule.** The *Schedule* slider is a row of 12 slots. Hover a cell and set it to 1, 2 or 3 to decide which transaction sends its next statement. Leftover statements run in turn after the last slot. Change the order and watch whether the anomaly survives.

> The ground truth is the **serializability check** at the end: does *any* one-at-a-time order of the same transactions produce the same reads and the same final table? An anomaly is precisely a schedule where the answer is no.

scenes.title: Isolation Levels
scenes.description: Replay the same schedule at each isolation level, under textbook locking and modelled PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and MongoDB.
scenes.markdown:
### Isolation levels: replay the same schedule

An isolation level is a promise about **which anomalies cannot happen**. This scene replays the **same anomaly schedules** from the previous scene — what changes is the database underneath. Pick an anomaly, keep its schedule, and move **Isolation level** and **Database**: the same statements now meet locks, snapshots or aborts. Two extra scenarios show the lost update fixed in the query itself (`FOR UPDATE`, atomic `UPDATE`).

| Level (ANSI / textbook) | Prevents | Typical mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Read Uncommitted | dirty writes | exclusive write locks held to commit |
| Read Committed | + dirty reads | readers wait for, or skip, uncommitted versions |
| Repeatable Read | + non-repeatable reads, lost updates | shared locks held to commit |
| Snapshot | reads from one consistent snapshot | MVCC + first-updater-wins |
| Serializable | everything | predicate locks, or SSI |

**Same names, different products.** The **Database** slider replays the schedule under a model of each product's documented behaviour:

- **PostgreSQL** never shows uncommitted data. *Repeatable Read* is snapshot isolation: a concurrent update aborts with `40001`, but **write skew is allowed**. *Serializable* is SSI: it aborts the write skew too.
- **MySQL / InnoDB** *Repeatable Read* (the default) reads a snapshot, but `UPDATE` acts on the newest row without a conflict check, so the read-modify-write **lost update succeeds silently**. Use `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` or `SET v = v - 30`.
- **SQLite** is always serializable: one writer at a time, and a reader whose snapshot is stale cannot become the writer (`SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT`).
- **MongoDB** transactions read a snapshot and abort immediately on a write conflict (`TransientTransactionError`); write skew is possible.

The **isolation matrix** (right) runs every anomaly scenario at every level for the selected database. Nothing in it is typed in: each cell is the result of running the engine. ✗ = anomaly happened · *abort* / *deadlock* = prevented by aborting one transaction · *waits* = prevented by blocking · ✓ = prevented without either.

> These are models of documented behaviour, simplified to single-row values and statement-level ticks. They reproduce each product's visible outcome for these schedules, not its internals.
scenes.prompt: You are a database-systems mentor preparing the learner for senior system-design interviews. Use the live board and the computed isolation matrix. Distinguish ANSI definitions from product behaviour precisely (PostgreSQL RR = snapshot isolation, InnoDB RR lost update, SQLite single writer, MongoDB snapshot transactions). Always say these are models of documented behaviour.

scenes.title: Concurrency Control Mechanisms
scenes.description: Two-phase locking, optimistic validation, MVCC snapshots, SSI and a single writer on the same transactions.
scenes.markdown:
### Concurrency control: wait, abort, or keep versions

Isolation says *what* is promised; concurrency control is *how*. Every mechanism below gives serializable results (except plain snapshot isolation), but they pay in different currencies.

| Mechanism | Conflicts are handled by | Costs |
|---|---|---|
| **Two-phase locking** | waiting for locks; deadlocks abort a victim | blocking, deadlocks, readers block writers |
| **Optimistic (OCC)** | validating at commit; stale readers abort | wasted work under contention |
| **MVCC · snapshot isolation** | versions for readers; first-updater-wins for writers | write skew, old versions to clean up |
| **MVCC · SSI** | SI + dependency tracking; cycles abort at commit | some false-positive aborts |
| **Single writer** | one writer at a time | no write concurrency at all |

Turn on **Retry aborted transactions** to see what an application does after `40001` / `40P01`: run the whole transaction again (see `retry.py` in the **Code** tab).

**In real systems**

- **PostgreSQL** — MVCC with tuple versions in the heap (old ones removed by `VACUUM`); row locks for writers; SSI at Serializable; deadlock detector aborts a victim.
- **MySQL / InnoDB** — MVCC through the undo log; record and **next-key (gap) locks** for locking reads and Serializable; a deadlock detector rolls back the smaller transaction.
- **SQLite** — a database-level write lock; in WAL mode readers keep a snapshot and never block the writer.
- **MongoDB (WiredTiger)** — document-level MVCC; a conflicting write aborts with `WriteConflict` and the driver's `withTransaction` retries.
- **DynamoDB** — no interactive transactions. Optimistic control is a **conditional write** on a version attribute; `TransactWriteItems` applies up to 100 actions atomically or cancels them all.
- **Redis** — commands run one at a time; `WATCH` + `MULTI/EXEC` is optimistic (EXEC fails if a watched key changed), and there is no rollback.

The **mechanism matrix** (right) runs the contention scenarios under every mechanism with retries on: *ticks to finish · aborts · wait ticks*, or ✗ when an anomaly survived.

scenes.description: Each concurrency-control algorithm as a flowchart: the path every statement takes lights up as the schedule runs.
scenes.markdown:
### Inside the algorithms

The board shows *what* happens; the flowchart beside it shows *how the algorithm decides*. Every tick, the statement that runs walks a path through the flowchart: the blocks it visits glow, the pipes between them light, and each block says what happened there ("T2 wants X(A); conflicts with S:T1"). Blocks it did not visit show what they are for.

Each step starts with one algorithm; move **Concurrency control** to switch the flowchart (and the simulation) to another, and change the **Workload** and **Schedule** freely. Open the **Code** tab for each algorithm's pseudocode: the lines of every visited block are highlighted, and clicking a block opens its line.

| Algorithm | The decision that matters |
|---|---|
| **Two-phase locking** | *Compatible with held locks?* — if not, wait; and every wait asks *is there a cycle?* |
| **Optimistic (OCC)** | Nothing is decided until commit: *did anything I read change since I started?* |
| **MVCC** | Reads pick a version and never wait; writes ask *did someone commit this row after my snapshot?* SSI adds *would my commit close a dependency cycle?* |
| **Single writer** | *Is the write lock free?* and *is my snapshot still current?* |

> These are teaching sketches of the algorithms. Real engines add many refinements (lock upgrades and intention locks, predicate locks at index granularity, SIREAD locks, group commit, …).
scenes.prompt: You are a database-internals mentor. The learner sees one concurrency-control algorithm as a flowchart beside the transaction board. Ground every explanation in the highlighted path and the block texts for the current tick. Ask the learner to predict which branch the next statement will take before revealing it. Connect each decision to the pseudocode in the Code tab, and say clearly that these are teaching sketches of the algorithms, not product source code.

guides.text: Each statement requests a lock. Follow **T1** and **T2** to the *Deadlock cycle?* check at tick 6: the answer is yes, so one becomes the victim.
Reads and writes never wait: writes go to a **private buffer**. At commit, *Changed since?* decides — the first committer wins, the others are thrown away and retried.
Reads take the *visible version* and never wait. The second writer passes the row lock but fails *Newer commit?* — first-updater-wins aborts it.
Write skew passes every write check. Under **SSI** the commit asks *Cycle?* — T2 would close one, so it aborts. Switch to snapshot isolation to see it commit.
Only one writer at a time. T2 finds the write lock free but its **snapshot stale** — T1 committed since — so it must restart before it may write.
